title: A morning intention
tomorrow: why did Thoreau call a swim in a pond a religious exercise?

cards: Before a run, people set a pace on their watch. Islam has an older kind of aiming, and it begins with a journey.
Sahih al-Bukhari opens its whole collection with Umar ibn al-Khattab on the pulpit, repeating what he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say.

It was about the hijra, the migration to Medina, a road that cost people their homes. And the Prophet names someone who makes the very same journey for another reason: a woman he wants to marry. Does his journey count?

teach.b: Here is the saying, in paraphrase. Actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. Whoever migrated for God and His Messenger, their migration is for God and His Messenger.
Whoever migrated for something of this world, or for a woman to marry, their migration is for what they migrated for.
Same road. Same dust. Same new city.
Two different journeys, and you can't tell them apart from the outside. Notice the man who traveled for love isn't cursed. He gets what he went for: a marriage.
The point is the aim. That's the teaching, and it has a name: niyyah, intention.

In Islamic teaching a prayer or a fast begins with niyyah, held in the heart; some say it in words too, others simply hold it. And by this hadith, even a meal or a day's work is weighed by the aim behind it.
A hadith ties the fast to an intention made before dawn.
So an ordinary act, aimed at something larger, becomes something larger.

Something to tell a friend tonight: of all the sayings he gathered, Bukhari chose this one to put first. On your own path, borrowed with the tag on: this morning's acts may look a lot like yesterday's.
The niyyah is what makes this day this day.

how: Muslims make a niyyah, an intention held in the heart, before prayer and before fasting; some also say it in words. Bukhari placed the hadith of intentions first in his collection.

o: a prediction of how the day is going to turn out
a list of tasks to check off before lunch
the aim you set in your heart before the day's acts

games.q: the hadith of intentions: tap the pairs.
p: migrated for a woman to marry

s: in the hadith, the man who traveled to marry is condemned
the hadith says he got what he went for. the point is the aim, not a curse.
in Islam, an intention only counts if you say it out loud
scholars place niyyah in the heart; some also say it in words.
Bukhari opens his collection with the hadith of intentions
of all the sayings he gathered, he put this one first.

games.q: two coworkers both stay late to finish a big order. one does it to help the team, one to impress the boss. by the hadith of intentions, what's true?
o: the same act, two different deeds: each gets what they aimed at.
the same act, so the same deed; only the finished order counts.
staying late is good either way, so the aims weigh the same.
games.why: actions are judged by intentions. from outside the road looks the same; the hadith weighs the aim.

practice: Rest one hand flat on your chest and feel it rise and fall for a few breaths. Then finish one sentence quietly, in your own words: today I will, and one aim, not a list.
Keep the hand there while you mean it, the way niyyah is held in the heart.

wordCard.voice: A morning intention: the aim you set before the acts. In Islam, niyyah: the same road, a different journey.

orig.note: Arabic: intention, the aim held in the heart before an act.

carryVoice: Your line: today I will. One aim, set in the heart before the day's first act. Sixteen hundred days, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1 (the hadith of intentions, narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab from the pulpit); the clause on migrating for God and His Messenger is in the fuller versions, Sahih al-Bukhari 54 and Sahih Muslim 1907
